sources.note: Nothing for Foya/Mander: the 'General information' header (p. 109) gives only location and the questionnaire number; the stress remarks in the volume (p. 30 'Stress placement usually on the ultimate or the penultimate'; the Awya header 'The stress falls mainly on the penultimate syllable or final syllable') belong to other lists (Moi, Awya), not to Foya.

sources.citation: Usher, Timothy. n.d. [2020-2022]. Orya-Tor River. New Guinea World (sites.google.com/site/newguineaworld), the Internet Archive snapshot 2022-10-06 (the live site is now login-gated)
sources.note: Only a proto-level remark ('Mid central schwa vowel /*ə/ has been found only in unstressed non-final syllables'); nothing on Mander/Jofotek word stress. Its source list confirms the whole documentary record for Mander/Jofotek is wordlists: Oosterwal 1961: 274-277; Voorhoeve 1975: 107; Stokhof 1983: 85-114 (Foya); Smits & Voorhoeve 1994; Lee & Wambaliau 2004: 40-62 (239 terms + 21 sentences for Jofotek of Biridua).

sources.citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 2007. Australasia and the Pacific. In Christopher Moseley (ed.), Encyclopedia of the World's Endangered Languages, 425-577. London: Routledge.
sources.note: Entry gives location (Upper Bu River, tributary of the Upper Tor), 'P, TNGP, Tor', 'For structural notes see the Bonerif entry' (Bonerif entry: 'Structurally the Tor languages correspond to the TNGP type, but have rudimentary gender distinction in verb forms, and directional markers'; the TNGP type note in the Damal entry says only that tones are 'phonologically relevant.. in many of them'), 20 speakers (1991), Berik as second language. No language-specific statement on word stress or tone.

sources.note: Nothing; Mander has zero descriptive (grammar/phonology/sketch) references — only overviews and wordlists (Voorhoeve 1975 x2, Oosterwal 1961, Smits & Voorhoeve 1994, Stokhof 1983, Stroeve 1911, Le Roux n.d.); Jofotek-Bromnya has only Lee & Wambaliau 2004 (overview; wordlist; socling, 'To appear in the SIL Electronic Survey Reports', 88 pp.).

sources.note: Mander is mentioned only as a Tor-Lake Plain relative of Orya with 26% cognates on a 200-word list and as a present-day contact group; the phonology (incl. Orya stress) is of Orya only; nothing on Mander prosody.

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Languages of Irian Jaya: Checklist. Preliminary classification, language maps, wordlists. Pacific Linguistics B-31. Canberra: ANU. (Mander = list 75, after Anceaux; 40-item wordlist on printed p. 107)
sources.note: Nothing. Mander appears only as a classification line (p. 11) and a 40-item comparative wordlist (p. 107, p. 111); the word 'stress' does not occur in the volume and the wordlist forms carry no stress marks.

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1971. Miscellaneous notes on languages in West Irian, New Guinea. In T. Dutton, C. L. Voorhoeve & S. A. Wurm, Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 14 (Pacific Linguistics A-28), 47-114. Canberra: Australian National University. (section 2.3.5, printed pp. 66-70: Tor Stock membership incl. Mander, lexicostatistics and Tami-Tor cognate sets using Oosterwal's 1961 Mander [MA] list)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone for Mander or any Tor language. The only Mander-specific phonological remark is segmental and comparative (p. 67): 'In many words MA retains an initial k which has been lost in other Tor languages.. The BO and MA forms contain an element -ne or -n which is found with several names of body parts.' Oosterwal's spelling is retained ('oe > u; ie > i'), so the forms carry no prosodic marking. The words 'tone/tones' in the volume belong to the notes on Sko.

sources.note: Nothing: a classification compendium that only lists 'Mander' and 'Foja' among Capell's Upper Tor River language names under Cowan's North Papuan Phylum; no data or phonology for any Tor language.

sources.citation: Oosterwal, Gottfried. 1961. People of the Tor: A cultural-anthropological study on the tribes of the Tor territory (Northern Netherlands New-Guinea). Assen: Van Gorcum. 322 pp.
sources.note: Ethnography with the earliest comparative wordlist covering Mander (pp. 274-277) and kin terms (pp. 218-286); may carry a note on pronunciation/orthography of the recorded forms.
